Theodicy. The philosophical and theological effort to justify the existence of evil and suffering in a world governed by an omnipotent, omniscient, and benevolent God. The term itself combines the Greek words for God and justice, and was coined by the philosopher Leibniz in the seventeenth century.

The classical formulation of the problem is deceptively simple: if God is omnipotent, He can prevent evil; if benevolent, He would want to; if omniscient, He foresees it. Yet evil exists—so how can all three divine attributes coexist with evil's reality?

Traditional theological responses include the free will defense, which argues that evil results from human freedom, which God permits to preserve genuine choice. Another approach is soul-making theodicy, the idea that suffering develops moral and spiritual growth through adversity.

Augustine's early theodicy emphasized human free will and the notion of evil as a privation of good—evil as absence rather than as a positive force in the world. Aquinas later refined this distinction between natural evil and moral evil, between suffering caused by circumstance and suffering caused by human choice.

The book of Job presents theodicy without resolving it. Job suffers unjustly, questions God, and receives no rational explanation—only a reassertion of God's incomprehensible power and sovereignty.

Leibniz argued this is the best of all possible worlds, a formulation later mocked by Voltaire in his novel Candide as naive optimism that ignores real suffering and natural disasters.

Modern theodicy often abandons the attempt to reconcile evil with omnipotence entirely. Process theology proposes that God is not omnipotent but co-creative with the world. Skeptical theism suggests that human cognitive limits simply prevent us from fully understanding divine purposes.

The distinction between moral and natural evil complicates theodicy further. The free will defense applies only to human cruelty and choice, not to disease, earthquakes, and suffering not caused by human will.
